lessons.title: Atomic Structure
lessons.objective: Distinguish atoms, molecules and ions, state the contributions of Dalton, Millikan, Rutherford, Moseley, Thomson and Bohr, count protons/neutrons/electrons from atomic and mass numbers, name the four quantum numbers and the rules for filling orbitals, describe s and p orbital shapes, and calculate relative atomic mass from isotopes.

content.heading: Atomic Structure
paragraphs: Everything you have ever touched — including you — is built from particles too small to see. Those particles come in shapes you already know from daily life: single beads, beads joined in pairs, and beads that have gained or lost a charge. Chemistry starts by naming those three shapes correctly.

content.heading: Atoms, molecules and ions in daily words
paragraphs: An atom is one single bead of an element, like one grain of rice. A molecule is atoms holding hands, like a short string of grains. An ion is an atom that has gained or lost an electron, so it carries a charge.

Protons are positive, neutrons neutral. H and He are atoms; H₂O is a molecule; Na⁺ is an ion. Dalton: indivisible atoms in whole-number ratios. Thomson: electron. Rutherford: tiny nucleus. Moseley: atomic number fixes identity. Millikan: charge e. Bohr: shells.
bullets: Atom: one single bead. Molecule: beads holding hands. Ion: a charged bead.
Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Moseley, Millikan, Bohr: one idea each.
content.takeaway: Atoms are single beads, molecules are joined beads, and ions carry a charge.

check.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the three particles?
options: Na is a molecule, Na+ is an atom and NaCl is an ion
Na is an atom, Na+ is an ion and NaCl is a formula unit of a compound
Na is an ion, Na+ is a molecule and NaCl is an atom
Na, Na+ and NaCl are all molecules
check.why: Na is a single atom, Na+ is that atom minus one electron, and NaCl is a formula unit, not a discrete molecule.

content.heading: Counting the three parts of an atom
paragraphs: Think of the atom as a class of people. The proton count names the element, like a school name tag. That count is the atomic number, Z. Protons plus neutrons is the mass number, A. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so electrons = Z.

Neutrons are simply what is left: neutrons = A − Z. Chlorine has Z = 17, so 17 protons and normally 17 electrons. Isotopes are family members differing only in neutrons, like ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. The relative atomic mass is the weighted average: (75 × 35 + 25 × 37) ÷ 100 = 35.5.
bullets: Z = protons = the element’s identity.
Neutrons = A − Z; electrons = Z when neutral.
RAM weights isotopes by abundance, not plain average.
content.takeaway: Z counts protons, A − Z counts neutrons, and abundance sets the average.

check.question: For 37Cl, how many protons and neutrons does one atom contain?
check.why: Chlorine has Z = 17, so protons = 17 and neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20.

content.heading: Shells, addresses and shapes
paragraphs: Electrons live on floors (shells) around the nucleus, in rooms called orbitals. Each electron has an address of four quantum numbers: n names the floor, l the room type, ml the exact room, and ms the spin direction.

Three rules govern filling. Aufbau fills the lowest rooms first, like front seats. Hund spreads electrons singly before pairing, like students taking separate seats. Pauli allows at most two electrons per room, spinning opposite ways.
An s orbital is a round cloud holding 2 electrons; a p subshell has three dumbbells holding 6. Chlorine (Z = 17) arranges as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ — count them: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17.
bullets: Shells are floors; orbitals are rooms; quantum numbers are addresses.
Aufbau: lowest first. Hund: singly first. Pauli: two at most.
s = round cloud (2); p = three dumbbells (6).
content.takeaway: Four quantum numbers address each electron, and three rules govern the filling.

check.question: Which set obeyed the Pauli principle for two electrons?
options: 1s2 with ms = +1/2 and -1/2 in the same orbital
1s3 with three electrons in one orbital
2p6 with all six electrons paired in one orbital
check.why: Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and they must have opposite spins.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any electron-configuration answer, write Z first and count your electrons to match it. Most lost marks come from a total that does not equal Z.

content.problem: Chlorine has isotopes Cl-35 (75%) and Cl-37 (25%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of chlorine.

steps.reason: Most atoms are Cl-35 and a quarter are Cl-37
Each mass is weighted by how common it is
Percentages must return to a per-atom average

content.question: Bromine has isotopes Br-79 (50%) and Br-81 (50%). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
hints: Multiply each mass by its percentage
Add the two products
Divide the sum by 100

content.heading: Go deeper: Why mass number and atomic number differ
paragraphs: Atomic number Z and mass number A answer different questions. Z asks what element it is — the proton count decides the family. A asks how heavy the atom is — protons plus neutrons. Two atoms can share the same Z and still have different A, which is exactly what isotopes are.

Chlorine shows the pair: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl both have Z = 17 but differ in neutrons (18 versus 20). Calcium-40 and argon-40 show the reverse: same A = 40, but different Z (20 versus 18), so they are different elements with the same mass.

That is why the periodic table is ordered by Z and not by A. Moseley's X-ray work showed Z fixes identity, and the occasional inversion in mass order (argon before potassium) disappears once Z takes over. Mass decides average weight; proton count decides identity.

A useful habit: read the numbers in order — top number A, bottom number Z in the usual symbol — and ask first what Z says, then what A adds. Most isotope errors come from reading the two numbers as one idea.
bullets: Z = identity; A = weight; they are not the same idea.
Same Z, different A = isotopes; same A, different Z = different elements.
The table is ordered by Z (Moseley), not by mass.
Read Z first, then ask what A adds.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the octet is stable
paragraphs: Atoms behave like small rooms whose outer shell wants eight electrons — the octet. Sodium (2,8,1) has one electron in its outer shell and loses it to become Na⁺ with a full (2,8) shell, which is why sodium reacts so eagerly. Chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to reach Cl⁻ (2,8,8), completing its octet.

Helium is the exception that proves the rule: its shell holds only two electrons (1s²), the duet, and it is completely inert. Noble gases are inert because their outer shells are already full, and other atoms become stable by matching that arrangement.

This one idea predicts bonding and ion formation. Elements on the left of the table lose electrons to reach a full shell; elements on the right gain them. Hydrogen and helium are the only elements that stop at two.

The octet also explains why metals are conductive and why some compounds form lattice structures: ions with full shells pack stably. Every later lesson on bonding leans on this idea, so it is worth understanding before moving on.
bullets: Outer shell wants 8 electrons (octet); helium wants 2 (duet).
Na loses 1 to fill its shell; Cl gains 1 to fill its own.
Reached-octet atoms are stable and unreactive.
Bonding predictions start from this rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in atomic structure
paragraphs: The commonest trap is swapping the two numbers: writing A as the proton count or Z as the mass. The question 'how many protons in ⁴⁰₂₀Ca?' tests exactly that: 20, from Z, not 40. Always hunt for Z first.

The second trap is the plain average of isotope masses. The RAM of chlorine is not (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36; it is abundance-weighted and equals 35.5. Averages in chemistry are weighted by how common each part is.

The third trap is electron-counting for ions. Na⁺ has 10 electrons, not 11, because losing one electron changes only the electron count — Z and A stay put. Cl⁻ has 18 electrons for the same reason in reverse.

The fourth trap is configuration totals. After writing a configuration, add the superscripts and check the sum against Z. A sum that does not match Z means the arrangement is wrong, no matter how neatly it looks.
bullets: Protons come from Z, never from A.
RAM is abundance-weighted, not a plain average.
Ions change electron count only; Z and A stay fixed.
Check configuration totals against Z every time.

lessons.title: Chemical Combination
lessons.objective: State the laws of definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions and conservation of mass, write chemical symbols, formulae and balanced equations, and perform mole-concept calculations (moles from mass, concentration, gas volume) and stoichiometry.

content.heading: Chemical Combination
paragraphs: A trader in Onitsha keeps one scale pan for rice and one for beans, and a customer always gets exactly what the scale says. Chemicals combine the same way: in fixed, weighable proportions. This lesson names the three laws behind those proportions and teaches counting by weighing.

content.heading: Three laws in plain words
paragraphs: Conservation of mass says matter is never created or destroyed, only rearranged. Twelve grams of carbon plus 32 grams of oxygen gives 44 grams of carbon dioxide, because 12 + 32 = 44. Nothing is lost.

The law of definite proportions says a compound always has the same mass ratio of its elements. Water is always 1 g of hydrogen to 8 g of oxygen. If the ratio changed, it would be a different compound.

The law of multiple proportions says that when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one combining with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple ratio. Twelve grams of carbon combines with 16 g of oxygen in CO and 32 g in CO₂ — a ratio of 1:2.
bullets: Mass in = mass out; reactions only rearrange matter.
Every compound has a fixed mass ratio of its elements.
Paired compounds use simple whole-number mass ratios.
content.takeaway: Mass is conserved, ratios are fixed, and paired compounds use simple ratios.

check.question: 12 g of carbon forms CO with 16 g of oxygen and CO₂ with 32 g. Which law do 16 and 32 illustrate?
check.why: For a fixed mass of carbon, the oxygen masses 16 and 32 are in the simple ratio 1:2.

content.heading: Formulae and balanced equations
paragraphs: A formula counts atoms: H₂O means two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Symbols are the shorthand — H for hydrogen, O for oxygen — and the subscript is the count. Writing the formula is writing the recipe.
A balanced equation has equal atoms on both sides, since atoms are only rearranged. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O has C1 H4 O4 on both sides. If counts differ, the equation lies about conservation.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula: divide each percentage by its Ar, then by the smallest value. A compound of 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3, which reduces to CH₂O.
bullets: A formula counts atoms; subscripts are counts.
Balancing means equal atom counts on both sides.
Percentage composition gives the empirical formula.
content.takeaway: Formulae count atoms, equations must balance, and percentages become formulae.

check.question: A compound is 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. What is its empirical formula?
check.why: Dividing by Ar (12, 1, 16) gives 3.3, 6.7, 3.3, so the ratio is 1:2:1.

content.heading: The mole: counting by weighing
paragraphs: One mole is a counting unit, like a dozen eggs: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. A mole of any substance has the same particle count, but different particles weigh differently, so a mole of carbon and a mole of water weigh different amounts.
Moles come from mass using moles = mass ÷ Mr. Methane has Mr = 16, so 0.5 mol weighs 8 g. One mole of any gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p., and concentration is moles ÷ volume.
Stoichiometry applies the equation’s mole ratio to real masses. Calcium carbonate (Mr = 100) gives one mole of CO₂ per mole, so 50 g is 0.5 mol and releases 11.2 dm³ of gas at s.t.p.
bullets: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, like a dozen eggs.
Moles = mass ÷ Mr; gas at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm³ per mole.
Stoichiometry applies the equation’s mole ratio.
content.takeaway: A mole counts particles by weighing, and equations give the ratios.

check.question: What is the mass of 0.5 mol of methane, CH₄ (Mr = 16)?
check.why: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.5 × 16 = 8 g.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Changed one unit? Convert cm³ to dm³ first (divide by 1000). Most mole errors in the hall are unit errors, not concept errors.

content.problem: Calculate the mass of 0.5 mol of methane, CH₄ (Mr = 16).

steps.reason: Mass is what weighs, moles is what counts, Mr links them
Half a mole of a Mr of 16 weighs half of 16 grams
A mole in this service is always 6.02×10²³ particles

content.question: Calculate the volume of 0.25 mol of a gas at s.t.p.
hints: One mole fills 22.4 dm³
Multiply 0.25 by 22.4
Check your units are dm³

content.heading: Go deeper: Why equations must balance
paragraphs: An equation is a scale pan: atoms on the left must equal atoms on the right, because reactions only rearrange. Unbalanced equations pretend atoms appear or vanish, which breaks conservation of mass. Balancing is therefore counting, not decoration.

The counting order that never fails: balance metals first, then non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen last. Metals rarely appear more than once per side, while oxygen and hydrogen hide inside several compounds and need final checking.

In CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O the carbon balances at once, hydrogen forces 2H₂O, and oxygen then forces 2O₂. Notice the coefficients: doubling H₂O also doubles its oxygen, which is why oxygen is adjusted last.

A systematic candidate counts each element across the whole arrow, not per compound. Total counts, not written counts, decide balance — that is the habit that prevents a balanced-looking equation from being wrong.
A candidate who counts totals before adjusting coefficients balances every equation on the first attempt. The habit costs seconds and saves whole marks.
The system also explains why fractional coefficients are tidied by multiplying the whole equation through: the atom totals do not change, only the presentation.
bullets: Balancing is counting: atoms are only rearranged.
Order: metals, non-metals, then oxygen and hydrogen.
Count totals across the whole arrow, not inside one compound.

content.heading: Go deeper: Empirical and molecular formulae compared
paragraphs: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the true count in one molecule. Glucose and fructose share the empirical formula CH₂O, but only glucose is written C₆H₁₂O₆. The ratio is the same; the size is not.

The link between them is the molar mass. CH₂O has Mr = 30 and glucose has Mr = 180, so 180 ÷ 30 = 6, meaning the true formula is six empirical units. Comparing Mr values converts one formula into the other without any new experiment.

Finding an empirical formula is the reverse journey: percentage composition gives the atom ratio directly, and a measured Mr then scales the ratio up to the molecular formula. Percentages alone can never give the true formula — they only give the ratio.
The exam trap is to stop at the ratio when a molar mass was given. If Mr appears anywhere in the question, the answer needs scaling. No Mr, no scaling: that is the whole discrimination.
Empirical formulae also predict percentage composition, so a candidate can move in either direction between ratio, percentages and true formula in one set of steps.
bullets: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = true count.
Scale ratio by Mr ÷ empirical Mr.
Percentages alone never give the molecular formula.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in mole calculations
paragraphs: The first trap is confusing Mr with relative atomic mass: Mr is for a molecule, Ar for an atom. Water's Mr is 18 (2 × 1 + 16), while oxygen's Ar is 16. Using the wrong one changes every mole count after it.

The second trap is skipping the ratio. Two moles of acid may need only one mole of base; multiplying by the equation's ratio comes before any concentration arithmetic. Which is limiting comes from the smaller mole count after dividing by coefficients.
The third trap is s.t.p. values quoted at the wrong temperature. The 22.4 dm³ molar volume belongs to 273 K and 1 atm; at any other temperature the gas law, not the memorised volume, must be used.

The fourth trap is unit mixing: cm³ against dm³, or grams against kilograms. Moles ÷ volume needs dm³, and examiners plant cm³ figures precisely to catch candidates who skip conversion. Convert first, calculate second — always.
Reading the question twice catches the last trap: state the units beside every number as you write, and the habit will expose mismatches before they mark you down.
bullets: Mr is per molecule; Ar is per atom.
Apply the equation ratio before concentrations.
22.4 dm³ belongs only to 273 K and 1 atm.
Convert cm³ to dm³ before dividing.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
lessons.objective: Apply kinetic theory to distinguish solids, liquids and gases, explain changes of state and Brownian movement, deduce the gas laws from their statements, use the ideal gas equation PV = nRT and vapour density, and state factors that make real gases deviate from ideal.

content.heading: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas
paragraphs: Steam rises off a pot of hot yam water, and smoke drifts across a food stall. Both are invisible particles in motion. This lesson explains how the movement of tiny particles explains solids, liquids, gases and every gas law.

content.heading: Particles in motion make solids, liquids and gases
paragraphs: Everything is made of particles that are always moving. In a solid they vibrate in fixed positions. In a liquid they slide past one another. In a gas they move freely everywhere, which is why a gas fills a room.

Melting is particles gaining enough energy to slip past each other. Boiling is energy high enough that particles escape from everywhere at once. Vapourisation, by contrast, escapes only from the surface, at any temperature.

Freezing locks particles into place, and condensation returns a gas to a liquid as it cools. Brownian movement is the visible proof: tiny smoke particles jiggle because invisible air particles keep bumping them.
bullets: Solids vibrate in place; liquids slide; gases move freely.
Boiling bubbles throughout; vapourisation escapes only from the surface.
Brownian movement shows invisible particles bumping visible ones.
content.takeaway: The speed of particles decides whether matter is solid, liquid or gas.

check.question: A puddle dries on a cool day without ever bubbling. Which change is this?
check.why: Vapourisation is escape from the surface at any temperature; boiling bubbles throughout.

content.heading: Six gas laws in daily words
paragraphs: Boyle’s law says squeezing a gas raises its pressure, like crowding a bus. Charles’s law says a gas grows when heated, because faster particles push harder. Gay-Lussac’s law says pressure rises with temperature in a sealed container.

Avogadro’s law says equal volumes hold equal particle numbers, so one mole of any gas fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p. Graham’s law says light gases diffuse faster, by the square root of the mass ratio. Dalton’s law says a mixture’s total pressure is the sum of each gas’s pressure.
Each law names which variable is held constant. Reading that condition is the whole skill of applying them.
bullets: Boyle: squeeze a gas and pressure rises.
Charles: heat a gas and volume rises (in kelvin).
Avogadro: equal volumes, equal numbers. Graham: light is faster. Dalton: pressures add.
content.takeaway: Pressure, volume and temperature trade off in fixed, predictable ways.

check.question: A gas is squeezed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to its pressure?
check.why: Boyle's law says P ∝ 1/V, so halving V doubles P at constant temperature.

content.heading: One equation that joins them
paragraphs: The ideal gas equation joins all the laws: PV = nRT. P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, T is temperature in kelvin, and R is a constant. It reads like a recipe: pressure × volume equals amount × temperature (with R).

One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at 273 K and 1 atm, which is the molar volume. The vapour density of a gas is Mr ÷ 2, so a vapour density of 16 means Mr = 32. That link turns a gas measurement into a mass.

Real gases misbehave at high pressure and low temperature, when particles are squeezed close enough that their size and attractions matter. An ideal gas is the strict rule; a real gas is the rule with exceptions.
bullets: PV = nRT joins pressure, volume, amount and temperature.
One mole fills 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.; vapour density = Mr ÷ 2.
Real gases deviate at high P and low T.
content.takeaway: PV = nRT turns any two measurements into the rest.

check.question: What volume does 1 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 273 K and 1 atm?
check.why: V = 1 × 0.082 × 273 ÷ 1 ≈ 22.4 dm³, the molar volume at s.t.p.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Convert every temperature to kelvin before any gas calculation. Using Celsius instead of kelvin is the single easiest way to fail a gas item.

content.problem: Calculate the volume occupied by 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 273 K and 1 atm, using R = 0.082 dm³·atm·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.

steps.reason: Volume is what is asked, so it goes alone
Half a mole at standard temperature holds half the molar volume
Pressure of 1 atm leaves the volume unchanged

content.question: Calculate the volume of 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 546 K and 1 atm, using R = 0.082 dm³·atm·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.
hints: Use V = nRT ÷ P as before
Twice the temperature should double the volume from the worked example

content.heading: Go deeper: Why heating makes particles move faster
paragraphs: Temperature is the average speed of particles. Heating a gas hands energy to its particles, so the average speed rises. That is why Charles's law works: faster particles collide harder and push out to a larger volume.

The same idea explains boiling and vapourisation. At the surface, the fastest particles can escape at any temperature, which is vapourisation. Boiling needs the whole liquid to reach the energy where particles escape from everywhere, including bubbles inside.

It also explains why a gas's pressure climbs in a sealed container: the particles hit the walls harder and more often. Gay-Lussac's law is just Charles's law felt on the container instead of measured as volume.
A candidate who pictures collisions instead of formulas can reconstruct every gas law from this one image: speed makes pushing power, and pushing power is pressure.
A candidate who pictures collisions instead of formulas can rebuild every gas law from this one image: speed makes pushing power, and pushing power is pressure.
The same picture explains why perfume spreads: the fastest molecules escape first and race across the room while slower ones lag behind.
Cooling runs the film backwards, slowing particles until some can no longer escape and must condense.
bullets: Temperature measures average particle speed.
Heating raises speed, so gases expand.
Pressure is the force of particles hitting walls.
Pictures of collisions replace memorised laws.

content.heading: Go deeper: Graham's law worked case for hydrogen and oxygen
paragraphs: Graham's law says the rate of diffusion of a gas follows the inverse square root of its molar mass: rate ∝ 1 ÷ √Mr. Hydrogen (Mr = 2) against oxygen (Mr = 32) gives a rate ratio of √(32 ÷ 2) = √16 = 4, so hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster.

In time terms, if oxygen takes 40 seconds to diffuse the same distance, hydrogen takes 40 ÷ 4 = 10 seconds. The lighter gas always wins the race, which is why ammonia fumes cross a classroom long before heavier vapours even start.
The same ratio governs effusion through a tiny hole. A leaking balloon loses hydrogen fastest, not because hydrogen is 'stronger', but because its light particles move quicker between collisions.
The exam trap is inverting the ratio. To correct it, ask first which gas is lighter; the lighter one must have the faster rate, so its number must come out larger.
bullets: Rate ratio = √(heavier Mr ÷ lighter Mr).
H₂ diffuses 4× faster than O₂ (√16 = 4).
The lighter gas always has the faster rate.
Effusion follows the same mass rule.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in gas calculations
paragraphs: The deadliest trap is temperature units. Charles's law and PV = nRT need kelvin; using Celsius compresses or stretches the answer by a huge factor. At 27 °C the correct temperature is 300 K, not 27, and that single slip re-scales every result by about eleven times.

The second trap is vapour density. Vapour density equals Mr ÷ 2, never Mr itself. A vapour density of 16 means a relative molecular mass of 32, not 16. The factor of two is the examiners' favourite silent divider.

The third trap forgets Boyle's condition. If pressure changes, Boyle's law cannot be applied until the temperature is confirmed constant. The question will always bury the condition in plain words like 'the mixture is kept cool'.

The fourth trap is partial pressure addition in the wrong direction: Dalton's law adds pressures of separate gases sharing one container, it does not share one gas's pressure across gases. Reading 'in the same vessel' is the cue to add.
bullets: Always convert to kelvin (27 °C = 300 K).
Vapour density = Mr ÷ 2, never Mr.
Boyle's law needs constant temperature stated or implied.
Dalton's law adds gases sharing one vessel.

lessons.title: Periodic Table
lessons.objective: Relate atomic number to position on the periodic table, relate properties of groups of elements, explain variation of ionisation energy, ionic radii, electron affinity, electronegativity and conductivities across periods and down groups, and identify the alkali metals, alkaline-earth metals, halogens, noble gases and transition metals.

content.heading: Periodic Table
paragraphs: Elements arranged by atomic number into periods and groups show repeating patterns. Position predicts properties and explains trends, so one table answers both where an element sits and how it behaves in reactions.

content.heading: From atomic number to families
paragraphs: A student finds chlorine listed as element 17 and wonders why it stands beside bromine and fluorine. The table is ordered by atomic number, the number of protons, so element 17 follows 16 and precedes 18. Each new row starts when a new electron shell begins to fill.

Rows are called periods, and columns are called groups. Elements in the same group share the same outer-electron arrangement, so they show similar chemistry. Sodium is in period 3 and group 1, while chlorine is in the same period 3 but group 17.

Families are groups with common names. Group 1 are the alkali metals, group 2 the alkaline-earth metals, group 17 the halogens and group 18 the noble gases. The d-block in the middle holds the transition metals.
bullets: Period = row; group = column.
Same group means similar outer electrons.
Families: 1 alkali, 2 alkaline-earth, 17 halogens, 18 noble gases.
content.takeaway: Position follows atomic number, and group predicts chemical family.

check.question: Why do sodium and potassium behave similarly?
options: They both have one outer electron
They both have the same atomic number
They both have the same number of shells
check.why: Same group means same outer-electron arrangement, so chemical behaviour repeats down the group.

content.heading: What changes across and down
paragraphs: A candidate is asked to order magnesium, sodium and chlorine by size and by ability to attract electrons. Across a period the atoms gain protons while electrons fill the same shell. Radii shrink, ionisation energy, electronegativity and electron affinity rise, and metallic character falls.

Down a group, each step adds a whole electron shell while nuclear charge rises more slowly. Atoms and ions get bigger, so ionisation energy and electronegativity fall. Metallic character grows, because larger atoms lose outer electrons more easily.

Electrical and thermal conductivity follow metallic character: metals are good conductors and non-metals are poor. Across a period, conductivity therefore falls as metallic character falls. Down a group, metallic character rises, but conductivity can dip slightly.
bullets: Across: radii fall; ionisation energy and electronegativity rise.
Down: radii rise; ionisation energy and electronegativity fall.
Metallic character falls across and rises down.
Conductivity tracks metallic character.
content.takeaway: Across a period atoms shrink and attract more strongly; down a group they enlarge and attract less.

check.question: Across period 3, which order is correct for atomic radius?
check.why: Radius falls across a period, so chlorine is smallest and sodium largest.

content.heading: Why trends happen and family behaviour
paragraphs: A student expects potassium, with more protons than sodium, to hold its outer electron tighter than sodium does. Yet potassium reacts faster with water. The extra inner shell shields the outer electron in potassium.

Across a period, nuclear charge increases with almost no extra shielding, so electrons are pulled closer and harder to remove. Down a group, a new shell is added, so shielding rises and the outer electron is farther from the nucleus. That distance and shielding explain larger radii and lower ionisation energy.

Alkali metals lose one electron easily and are therefore very reactive. Halogens are non-metals that gain one electron to form negative ions. Noble gases have full outer shells and are inert, while transition metals form variable oxidation states and act as catalysts.
bullets: More shielding weakens the pull.
Alkali metals: reactive, lose one electron.
Halogens: non-metals, form negative ions; noble gases inert.
Transition metals catalyse; oxidation states vary.
content.takeaway: Shielding and distance weaken the pull down a group; full shells make noble gases inert.

check.question: Why do atoms get larger down a group despite more protons?
options: A new electron shell is added
Electrons move to the same shell
check.why: Each step down adds a shell, so distance and shielding outweigh the extra protons.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For trend questions, always state the direction first, then the reason in one line. Say across a period electronegativity increases because nuclear charge rises with little extra shielding. Do not reverse the direction down a group.

content.problem: Arrange sodium, magnesium and chlorine in order of increasing electronegativity and give the reason.

steps.reason: Electronegativity follows position from left to right across a period.
Nuclear charge rises while shielding stays nearly constant.
The leftmost element attracts least, the rightmost most.

content.question: Arrange potassium, sodium and lithium in order of increasing ionisation energy and explain the trend.
hints: They are in the same group, so compare down the group.
Each step down adds a whole electron shell.
More shielding and distance mean weaker pull, so energy falls.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionisation energy rises across a period but falls down a group
paragraphs: Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom, so anything that strengthens the attraction between the nucleus and that electron raises the value. Across a period the outer shell stays the same while protons are added. Each new proton adds positive charge without adding a new inner shell to shield it.

The effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electron therefore grows steadily from left to right, pulling the electron closer and making it harder to remove. This is why first ionisation energy rises across period 3 from sodium through magnesium, aluminium and the p-block elements. The chemical consequence is that the right-hand elements hold their electrons tightly and tend to gain rather than lose them.

Down a group the picture reverses because each element adds a complete inner shell of electrons. That extra shell shields the outer electron, so the increased nuclear charge is largely cancelled, and the outer electron sits farther away. A more distant, better shielded electron experiences a weaker attraction and needs less energy to escape.

This explains the steady fall in first ionisation energy down group 1 from lithium to caesium, despite the larger proton number lower down. Small irregularities appear where electron pairing or a filled subshell creates extra stability, and examiners sometimes test those exceptions. The underlying rule remains that shielding and distance dominate the group trend, while rising nuclear charge dominates the period trend.
bullets: Across: effective nuclear charge rises, distance stays similar.
Down: shielding rises, distance grows, pull weakens.
Pairing and filled subshells cause small exceptions.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why atomic radius shrinks across a period but grows down a group
paragraphs: Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outer electron cloud, so any force that pulls the cloud inward shrinks it. The two competing forces are the attraction from protons and the shielding effect of inner electrons. Their balance decides whether the atom gets smaller or larger as position changes.

Across a period electrons enter the same outer shell while the nucleus gains a proton at each step. Shielding barely changes because the new electrons are in the same shell as the one being pulled, so effective nuclear charge rises sharply. The stronger pull outweighs electron-electron repulsion, and the cloud contracts, which is why sodium is larger than magnesium and magnesium larger than chlorine.

Down a group each successive element adds a complete new shell, so the outer electrons occupy a higher level that is inherently farther from the nucleus. That extra shell also shields the outer electrons, reducing the effective pull even though the proton number is larger. Distance therefore wins, and lithium is smaller than sodium, which is smaller than potassium and rubidium.

Ionic radii follow the same two rules but start from charged sizes, so they shrink across a period and expand down a group. Anions are larger than their parent atoms because gained electrons repel, while cations are smaller because fewer electrons share the same pull. Remembering the shell count therefore predicts both atomic and ionic size without memorising separate tables.
bullets: Across: same shell, more protons, stronger pull, smaller atom.
Down: new shell, more shielding, weaker pull, larger atom.
Cations shrink, anions swell relative to parent atoms.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in metallic character and electronegativity directions
paragraphs: Many candidates lose marks by giving right facts with opposite arrows, because two trends move together and two move apart. Metallic character falls across a period while electronegativity rises, so the leaders are opposite edges of the table. Down a group metallic character rises while electronegativity falls, so mixing those directions is the commonest trap.

Metallic character means tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions, which is strongest at the left where ionisation energy is low. Electronegativity means tendency to attract electrons and form negative ions, which is strongest at the right where effective nuclear charge is high. The two properties therefore point to opposite ends of a period, while conductivity follows metallic character and fades to the right.

Examiners exploit the confusion by asking for the group with the most metallic element or the element with the lowest electronegativity. The answer is usually the bottom-left group, not the top-right, because size and shielding dominate down a group. A second trap reverses conductivities, claiming non-metals conduct better than metals, which contradicts the delocalised electron sea in metals.

The safe method is to write both arrows vertically before answering, then match each property to its arrow. State position first, such as down group 17, and then give the value direction in words. If a question mentions electron affinity, add the warning that the trend generally rises across but has genuine exceptions such as chlorine over fluorine.
bullets: Metallic character falls across, rises down; electronegativity rises across, falls down.
Conductivity follows metallic character, not electronegativity.
Write both arrows before answering any trend question.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrovalent (ionic), covalent, coordinate, hydrogen, metallic bonds and van der Waals forces, deduce bond types from electron configurations, relate bonding to properties of compounds, and differentiate the shapes of simple molecules (linear, non-linear, tetrahedral, pyramidal).

content.heading: Chemical Bonding
paragraphs: Chemical bonding explains why atoms join and how the join decides hardness, conductivity and shape. Ionic, covalent, metallic, hydrogen, coordinate and van der Waals interactions each leave a different fingerprint in melting point, conduction and molecular geometry.

content.heading: Electrovalent (ionic) and covalent bonds
paragraphs: A learner melts table salt, and the bulb lights only when the salt is liquid, never as a cold solid. That contrast reveals electrovalent (ionic) bonding, where ions sit in a fixed lattice.

Electrovalency is electron transfer from metal to non-metal so each atom attains a stable noble-gas octet. Sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na+ (2,8), and chlorine (2,8,7) gains it to become Cl− (2,8,8). The opposite charges attract strongly, forming NaCl lattice rather than discrete molecules.

Covalency contrasts with transfer because atoms share electron pairs to complete octets. Oxygen shares two pairs with hydrogen in H2O, and carbon shares four pairs with hydrogen in CH4, giving neutral low-melting molecules.
bullets: Ionic bond: transfer of electrons to attain noble-gas octet structure (NaCl)
Covalent bond: sharing of electron pairs to complete octets (H2O, CH4)
Ionic compounds have high melting points, dissolve in water and conduct when molten or aqueous
content.takeaway: Ionic bonds transfer electrons for noble-gas stability; covalent bonds share pairs to complete octets.

check.question: Which pair of statements best explains NaCl and CH4?
options: NaCl is covalent because both atoms share electrons, and CH4 is ionic because carbon transfers electrons
NaCl is ionic because electrons transfer to complete octets, and CH4 is covalent because electrons are shared
Both are ionic because both contain polar bonds
Both are covalent because both contain discrete molecules
check.why: Transfer gives ionic NaCl and sharing gives covalent CH4, so only the second statement matches.

content.heading: Metallic, hydrogen, coordinate and van der Waals attractions
paragraphs: A copper wire bends and carries current, while ice warms and melts beside it. Copper's strength and conductivity come from metallic bonding, not shared pairs. Ice's easy melting comes from weak forces between molecules, not strong O–H covalent bonds.

Hydrogen bonding attracts H attached to N, O or F in one molecule to N, O or F in another. Water, HF and NH3 therefore boil unusually high. Van der Waals forces are weaker attractions between all molecules, e.g. H2, O2 and Cl2 at low temperature.

A coordinate (dative) bond shares both electrons from one atom. In [Fe(CN)6]3− and [Fe(CN)6]4−, cyanide donates to iron; in [Cu(NH3)4]2+ and [Ag(NH3)2]+, ammonia donates to copper and silver. The donor is the ligand.
bullets: Metallic bonding: ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, giving conduction
Hydrogen bonding occurs in water, HF and NH3
Van der Waals forces are weak, non-directional attractions between neutral molecules
content.takeaway: Metallic, hydrogen, coordinate and van der Waals bonds differ by electron source and strength.

check.question: Which set lists complexes containing coordinate bonds?
check.why: Cyanide and ammonia donate both electrons to the metal ion, which defines coordinate bonding.

content.heading: Shapes of simple molecules and bonding effects
paragraphs: A learner plots CO2 and water on the same board and finds one straight and one bent. The difference is not the atoms alone but the electron arrangement around the centre. Shape therefore records bonding and repulsion, not just atom count.

Linear molecules H2, O2, Cl2, HCl and CO2 place atoms at 180°, as in O=C=O. H2O is bent (non-linear) because lone pairs on oxygen repel bonds, closing the angle. CH4 is tetrahedral, while NH3 is trigonal pyramidal due to its lone pair.

Bonding fixes bulk properties too: in diamond each carbon joins four neighbours in a rigid network. In graphite, strong bonding within layers alternates with weak forces between layers, so layers slide. Hardness and conductivity therefore differ between the two forms.
bullets: Linear: H2, O2, Cl2, HCl, CO2 at 180°
Bent: H2O non-linear; tetrahedral: CH4; pyramidal: NH3
Shape follows bonding and lone-pair repulsion around the central atom
content.takeaway: Linear, bent, tetrahedral and pyramidal shapes follow bonding and lone-pair repulsion.

check.question: Which assignment of shapes is correct?
options: CO2 bent, H2O linear, CH4 pyramidal
CO2 linear, H2O bent, CH4 tetrahedral
HCl tetrahedral, NH3 linear, O2 bent
CH4 linear, CO2 tetrahedral, H2O pyramidal
check.why: CO2 is linear, H2O is bent, CH4 is tetrahedral and NH3 is trigonal pyramidal.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Count electrons gained and lost before naming the bond: transfer of one or more electrons means ionic, sharing means covalent, and donation of both electrons from one atom means coordinate. That electron count decides the answer faster than memorised compound names.

content.problem: Magnesium is 2,8,2 and chlorine is 2,8,7. Predict the formula and bond type of magnesium chloride.

steps.reason: Magnesium loses two electrons to reach 2,8; each chlorine gains one to reach 2,8,8
One Mg2+ charge balances two Cl− charges for neutrality
Electrons were transferred from metal to non-metal to attain octet stability

content.question: Calcium (2,8,8,2) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7). Predict the formula and bond type, explaining electrons lost and gained.
hints: How many electrons must calcium lose to reach 2,8,8?
How many electrons does each chlorine gain to reach 2,8,8?
How many chlorine atoms balance calcium's charge?

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionic solids conduct only when molten or dissolved
paragraphs: A crystal of sodium chloride contains ions, yet it does not conduct because every ion is locked at a fixed site in the lattice. Current needs moving charge carriers, and a solid lattice offers no free path. The absence of conduction in the solid therefore does not mean the compound lacks ions.

Melting supplies enough thermal energy to break the lattice order while keeping the ions together as a liquid. Molten sodium chloride then lets Na+ drift to the cathode and Cl− to the anode under voltage. The ions move toward opposite electrodes, complete the circuit and carry charge through the liquid.

Dissolving in water also separates the lattice because polar water pulls ions apart into mobile hydrated ions. Aqueous sodium chloride conducts for the same reason as the melt, while solid salt still fails. The test in JAMB is therefore about ion mobility, not ion existence: mobility appears only after melting or dissolving.
bullets: Solid ionic: ions fixed in lattice, so no conduction
Molten ionic: lattice breaks, ions move to electrodes, conduction occurs
Aqueous ionic: water separates ions into mobile hydrated ions
Melting or dissolving frees ions, so both methods reveal ionic conduction

content.heading: Go deeper: Hydrogen bonding versus dipole and van der Waals forces
paragraphs: All three forces are electrostatic attractions, but their sources differ in strength and place. Van der Waals forces come from temporary uneven electron clouds that induce matching poles in neighbours. They act between every molecule, including noble gases and chlorine, because momentary polarisation makes them weak and short range.

Dipole forces arise when a molecule has a permanent uneven charge distribution, as in hydrogen chloride or water. Opposite ends of neighbouring dipoles attract in fixed orientations, so the attraction is stronger and more directional than van der Waals forces. Yet dipole forces still involve whole molecules rather than a hydrogen attached directly to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.

Hydrogen bonding is the special dipole case where hydrogen is bound to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine and points toward a lone pair on nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine in another molecule. That geometry makes it much stronger than ordinary dipoles and explains why water, HF and ammonia associate through networks. Breaking that network needs extra heat, so boiling points rise well above expectation from size alone.
bullets: Van der Waals: temporary, weak, between all neutral molecules
Dipole forces: permanent poles attract directionally by alignment
Hydrogen bonding: strongest, needs H on N, O or F
Strength order helps prediction: hydrogen bonding exceeds dipole forces, which exceed van der Waals forces

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in deducing bonds from electron counts
paragraphs: The common trap is naming a bond from the element names before checking electron numbers. A metal with few outer electrons and a non-metal close to an octet often transfer, as in sodium and chlorine. Two non-metals at a distance from octets usually share instead, as in oxygen and hydrogen, so counting shells first makes the choice mechanical.

Another trap confuses coordinate bonding with ordinary covalent bonding because both involve sharing. The test is the source of the pair: a coordinate bond gives both electrons from one partner, as in ammonia donating to silver in [Ag(NH3)2]+. If both partners supply one electron each, the bond is ordinary covalent even when the species is a complex.

A third trap treats every strong attraction as ionic or every weak one as van der Waals. Metallic bonding is strong yet conducts as a solid because its electrons are delocalised. Hydrogen bonding is weak per bond but raises boiling points through many links, so judging by electron behaviour rather than strength alone avoids these errors.
bullets: Transfer of electrons to octets points to ionic bonding
Sharing one electron each points to ordinary covalent bonding
Both electrons from one partner points to coordinate bonding
Solid ionic conduction fails because ions cannot migrate until melted or dissolved

lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
lessons.objective: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures, differentiate chemical from physical changes, distinguish pure from impure substances, use melting/boiling points as purity criteria, and specify the principle and everyday use of each separation method (evaporation, distillation, sublimation, re-crystallisation, chromatography, crystallisation, magnetisation, decantation, filtration, centrifugation).

content.heading: Separation of Mixtures
paragraphs: Farmers in Lagos dry sea-water to recover salt, yet the salt water looks like one liquid. A mixture keeps the properties of its parts, so each part can be pulled out by a physical method.

content.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
paragraphs: A seller scoops salt from dried sea-water and asks whether salt and water were chemically bonded. An element is one kind of atom, such as iron. A compound joins elements in fixed ratio, such as water (H2O), while a mixture joins substances without a chemical bond.

A chemical change forms new substances hard to reverse, like rusting and burning. A physical change only alters state or form, like melting, dissolving or boiling. Separation uses physical change, so a mixture splits without new compounds.

A pure substance contains one element or one compound and melts and boils sharply. Dissolved impurities make water impure and broaden melting, freezing and boiling ranges. A sharp melting or boiling point and fixed density therefore test purity.
bullets: Compounds split into elements; mixtures split into parts
Mixtures keep the properties of their parts
Chemical change gives new substances; physical change does not
content.takeaway: A sharp melting point marks a pure substance.

check.question: Which sample is a pure substance?
check.why: Distilled water has one compound and boils sharply, while the others are mixtures.

content.heading: Separation by heating
paragraphs: A family needs drinking water but the borehole water is salty and cloudy. Evaporation heats the mixture so the liquid becomes vapour and leaves the solid residue, as sea-water dries to salt. Simple distillation boils the mixture then condenses the vapour to pure liquid for one boiling point.

Fractional distillation suits liquids with different boiling points, such as crude oil. The fractionating column lets the most volatile fraction rise highest, condensing petrol lower down and diesel lower still. Sublimation is solid to vapour without melting, used for camphor and ammonium chloride (NH4Cl), which deposit as solid on cooling.

Re-crystallisation dissolves the solid in hot solvent then cools it so crystals form. The solid is more soluble when hot and crystallises out first. Sugar refining uses this temperature change in solubility.
bullets: Evaporation leaves solid; distillation collects vapour
Fractional distillation needs different boiling points
Sublimation skips liquid; re-crystallisation uses solubility
content.takeaway: Heat methods separate by boiling point or solubility differences.

check.question: Crude oil contains petrol, kerosene and diesel. Which method separates it in one run?
check.why: The fractions differ greatly in boiling point, so fractional distillation separates them level by level.

content.heading: Separation by magnetism, density and absorption
paragraphs: A student tests mixed ink on paper and sees several spots spread apart. Paper chromatography moves each dye a different distance with the solvent, so the spots identify each part. Column chromatography adsorbs parts differently on a column, as in dye analysis.

Crystallisation evaporates solvent until crystals of the dissolved solid appear, like salt from brine. Magnetisation pulls magnetic iron from sand with a magnet, as in scrapyards. Decantation gently pours the clear liquid from settled solids, as cloudy water is poured from mud.

Filtration holds back insoluble solid on filter paper while liquid passes, as sand is filtered from salt solution. Centrifugation spins the mixture so denser parts settle quickly by density, as in blood tests. Choose by property: magnetism for iron, density for settling, insolubility for filtering.
bullets: Chromatography separates by adsorption and distance
Magnetisation uses magnetism; centrifugation uses density
Filtration holds insolubles; crystallisation recovers dissolved solids
content.takeaway: Match the method to the differing property of components.

check.question: Ink contains several dyes that travel different distances on paper. Which method separates them?
check.why: Paper chromatography moves each dye a different distance with the solvent, giving identifying spots.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When JAMB gives a mixture, name the differing property first: boiling point, solubility, density, magnetism or adsorption, then choose the method that uses it. Boiling together means fractional distillation, magnetic means magnetisation, dissolved solid means crystallisation.

content.problem: A mixture of sand, salt and water is given. Which methods separate all three, and in what order?

steps.reason: Sand is insoluble and stays on the paper while salt solution passes.
steps.result: Sand is left on filter paper; salt solution passes through.

steps.reason: Salt is dissolved, so heating drives off water and leaves salt behind.
steps.result: Water vapour escapes and dry salt remains in the dish.

steps.operation: Distill if pure water is needed
steps.reason: For pure water, boil the solution and condense the vapour separately.
steps.result: Distilled water is collected and salt stays in the flask.

content.question: A mixture of iron filings, sand and salt water is given. Outline methods to recover iron, sand, salt and water.
hints: First pick out the magnetic part with a magnet.
Then filter the remaining mixture to hold back the insoluble solid.
Evaporate or distil the solution to leave salt and collect water.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fractional distillation beats simple distillation
paragraphs: Simple distillation suits one boiling point, such as separating water from an involatile salt, and its vapour condenses straight to pure liquid in one collection. Fractional distillation suits several boiling points because it separates each component at its own temperature level. The fractionating column provides the extra surfaces that make that level-by-level separation possible.

Each glass bead in the column is a surface where vapour condenses and re-evaporates repeatedly. Higher-boiling vapours condense lower down while lower-boiling vapours stay as vapour and rise higher. The column therefore holds a temperature gradient, hot at the base and cool at the top, and each fraction is drawn off where that temperature matches its boiling point.

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons with widely spaced boiling points, so simple distillation yields a mixed distillate that must be repeated. Fractional distillation of crude oil gives gases at the top, petrol in the cooler upper zone, kerosene below it and diesel and lubricating oils lower still. The same column separates liquid air into nitrogen, oxygen and argon.
bullets: Simple distillation: one boiling point, one product
Fractional distillation: many boiling points, many products
Column holds a temperature gradient from hot base to cool top
Crude oil and liquid air need fractional distillation

content.heading: Go deeper: Rf values as identity evidence in chromatography
paragraphs: Paper chromatography is a partition and adsorption balance between the moving solvent and the stationary paper fibres and water. Each dye must repeatedly dissolve in the solvent front and adsorb onto the paper, spending different fractions of time in each phase. A dye that spends more time in the mobile solvent moves further with the front, while a strongly adsorbed dye lags behind.

The retardation factor, Rf, quantifies that movement as the distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front from the same origin. If a dye spot reaches 3.0 cm when the solvent reaches 10.0 cm, its Rf is 0.30. Rf is a ratio, so it is independent of paper size and strip length, which lets values be compared between different runs.

Identity is claimed only when an unknown spot has the same Rf as a known standard run on the same paper under the same conditions. Matching Rf plus spot colour and shape is evidence that the unknown contains that dye, as in food-colour and forensic ink tests. A different Rf rules out identity, while an extra spot reveals an additional component that a single colour would hide.
bullets: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent front
Same Rf as a standard on the same paper suggests identity
An extra spot means an extra component is present

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in purity and sublimation
paragraphs: A pure solid melts sharply at a fixed temperature because every particle needs the same energy to break its lattice. Dissolved impurities break up the lattice and lower the melting point while widening the melting range. A sample that melts over several degrees and below the reference value is therefore impure, even if it looks like a pure crystal.

Sublimation is a direct solid-to-vapour change without liquid, shown by camphor, naphthalene and ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) on gentle heating. Evaporation is liquid-to-vapour change at the surface of a liquid, shown by wet clothes drying or sea-water drying to salt. The trap is that both produce vapour, but sublimation starts from a solid and deposits solid on cooling, while evaporation leaves a non-volatile residue.

Examiners also trap candidates who call a melting mixture pure because it melts, or who claim boiling point is constant for salt solution. Salt solution boils over a range above 100 °C, not sharply at 100 °C, because dissolved salt lowers vapour pressure. Always ask whether the point is sharp and at the reference value before calling a substance pure.
bullets: Impurities depress the melting point and broaden the range
Sublimation: solid to vapour; evaporation: liquid to vapour
Salt solution boils over a range, not sharply at 100 °C

lessons.title: Solubility
lessons.objective: Distinguish unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions, interpret solubility curves, calculate the amount of solute that dissolves at a given temperature, relate solvents to their uses, and differentiate true solutions from suspensions and colloids with examples.

content.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: A trader in Kano asks why sugar vanishes in hot tea but fog still hangs in the air. This lesson separates solutions that can hold more, those that are full, and mixtures that only look dissolved.

content.heading: Unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions
paragraphs: A student stirs sugar into water and it vanishes at once, then stirs more until grains refuse to dissolve. That refusal marks saturation, while the earlier stage was unsaturated and choosing the right dose matters. Unsaturated solution holds less than the maximum at that temperature, saturated holds the maximum and supersaturated holds more than the maximum.

Most salts rise with temperature because warming helps the solid break its lattice, so hot water dissolves more. Gases fall with temperature because warm water holds less dissolved gas, which is why fizzy drinks go flat faster on a hot day. A solubility curve plots grams dissolved per 100 cm³ of water against temperature, so a point below the curve is unsaturated, on the curve is saturated and above the curve is supersaturated.
bullets: Unsaturated holds less than the maximum; saturated holds the maximum; supersaturated holds more.
Read solubility at a temperature directly from the curve.
Most salts rise with temperature; gases fall with temperature.
content.takeaway: Below the curve is unsaturated, on it saturated, above it supersaturated.

check.question: A solution holds more solute than the maximum at that temperature. What is it?
check.why: Holding more than the maximum means the solution is supersaturated.

content.heading: Solubility in mol/dm³ and solvents for stains
paragraphs: A dyer in Kano finds grease on a sleeve and wonders why water alone will not lift it. She needs two ideas: how much dissolves in a given volume and which liquid dissolves that dirt. Molar solubility is moles of solute dissolved per dm³ of solution at saturation, so c = n ÷ V with n = m ÷ M.

A solvent dissolves a stain only when like dissolves like: polar water lifts polar sweat and salts. Oils, grease and most paints need organic solvents such as petrol or turpentine because they share non-polar character. That match decides the cleaner, not the strength of the liquid.
bullets: Find moles first with n = m ÷ M, then divide by volume in dm³.
Water removes sweat and water-soluble stains; organic solvents remove grease and paint.
Petrol and turpentine are typical organic solvents for fats and paint.
content.takeaway: Convert mass to moles, divide by volume, and match solvent to stain.

check.question: Which solvent best removes engine grease from cloth?
check.why: Grease is non-polar like petrol, so petrol dissolves it while water does not.

content.heading: True solutions, suspensions and colloids
paragraphs: During Harmattan, dust hangs in the air all day and light looks milky, yet the dust later settles on roofs. A true solution like sugar water shows no such haze and passes filter paper without leaving residue. Suspensions such as Harmattan haze and water paints hold large visible particles that settle, while colloids scatter light but settle slowly.

Particle size decides the test: true particles are molecular and invisible, colloids are larger and show the Tyndall effect, and suspension particles are largest and visible to the eye. Fog, milk, blood, aerosol spray, emulsion paints and rubber solution all scatter a beam and resist ordinary filtration, unlike true solutions. Suspensions settle on standing and are held by filter paper, while colloids stay dispersed much longer.
bullets: True solution: invisible particles, no Tyndall, passes filter, never settles.
Suspension: visible particles, settles on standing, held by filter.
Colloid: shows Tyndall, scatters light, resists filtration, settles slowly.
Particle size and settling decide which of the three mixtures you have.
content.takeaway: True passes and hides, colloid scatters, suspension settles and blocks.

check.question: Which mixture is a colloid?
check.why: Fog scatters light and resists filtration like other colloids, unlike the suspensions and true solution.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: On curves, read the exact temperature first and check whether the curve slopes up or down. For mixtures, ask about particle size and settling before naming it. That pair of checks answers most solubility and colloid items directly.

content.problem: 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

steps.reason: Molar solubility needs moles, so convert mass to moles with M = 58.5 g/mol.
Molar solubility is moles per dm³ of solution, so divide by 0.1 dm³.
The value 1.880 mol/dm³ rounds to 1.88 mol/dm³ to two decimal places.

content.question: 5.85 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.5 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.
hints: Find moles with n = 5.85 ÷ 58.5.
Divide the result by 0.5 dm³.
Check the units are mol/dm³.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why gases dissolve less when warm
paragraphs: A gas has no crystal lattice to break apart, so dissolving it is mainly about holding its molecules inside water. Gas molecules are kept in solution only by weak attractions while water molecules move and jiggle around them. Warming gives those gas molecules more kinetic energy to escape the weak holds and return to the air above the liquid.

The dissolving of a gas releases heat, so the process is exothermic and heat is a product of the reaction. Adding heat therefore drives the balance back toward the undissolved gas instead of the dissolved form. That is why warm fizzy drinks lose their bubbles faster and why fish suffer when hot water cannot hold enough dissolved oxygen.

Solubility curves show the difference plainly because gases slope downward while most salts slope upward. A salt must pay energy to break its lattice, which warming supplies, so more solid can dissolve. A gas needs no such payment, so warming only helps it escape, which means curves must be read with the nature of the solute in mind.

Pressure matters for gases in a way it rarely does for salts, because pressing gas above a liquid forces more of it to dissolve. Closing a soft drink under pressure keeps gas inside until the seal is broken, while opening lets it rush out. Cooling together with pressure is therefore the recipe for keeping as much gas as possible in solution.
bullets: Gas dissolving is exothermic, so warming drives gas out.
Salts need lattice energy, so warming helps them dissolve.
Curves slope down for gases and up for most salts.
Higher gas pressure forces more gas to dissolve.

content.heading: Go deeper: Making and breaking a supersaturated solution
paragraphs: A supersaturated solution holds more solute than the equilibrium maximum at that temperature, so it is stable only until it is disturbed. The extra solute wants to come out as solid, but no new crystal forms on its own in a clean, still liquid. That delay makes the solution metastable, which means it looks normal yet sits ready to crystallise at the slightest trigger.

The usual way to make one is to dissolve as much salt as possible in hot water, filter off any excess, and then cool the clear liquid very gently. As the liquid cools, the maximum solubility falls, yet the dissolved amount stays at the hot value. The liquid is now above its new curve, so it holds more than it should at that temperature.

A single seed crystal, a scratch on the glass, or even a speck of dust gives the extra solute a surface to join. Crystals then grow rapidly and excess solute leaves the liquid until the concentration falls back to the saturated line. That rapid growth is why supersaturated samples sometimes turn cloudy in seconds after looking perfectly clear.

Careful cooling in clean containers avoids early crystallisation, while rough stirring or shaking invites it almost at once. The same idea explains why a hot saturated solution left to stand may deposit crystals on its own. Any time the dissolved amount sits above the curve, the solution is supersaturated and will soon correct itself unless it is protected.
bullets: Supersaturation is more dissolved solute than the curve allows.
Make it from a hot saturated solution cooled gently.
A seed crystal or scratch triggers rapid crystallisation.
Crystals grow until the solution falls back to saturation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in solubility and mixtures
paragraphs: Solubility and concentration sound alike but answer different questions, and mixing them is a favourite trap. Solubility is the maximum that can dissolve at a stated temperature, while concentration is the amount actually present, which may sit below that maximum. An unsaturated solution can be fairly concentrated yet still below its limit, so calling every strong solution saturated loses the mark.

A second trap is reading the wrong slope on a solubility curve. Most salts rise with temperature, so a falling curve usually signals a gas such as oxygen or carbon dioxide. Candidates who assume every curve rises will predict more gas in warm water and miss the correct fall. Naming the solute first decides which direction to expect.

Colloids and suspensions are separated by particle size, not by whether they look cloudy. Suspension particles are large, visible to the eye, settle on standing, and are held by ordinary filter paper. Colloid particles are far smaller, invisible to the eye, scatter light in the Tyndall effect, resist filtration, and stay dispersed for much longer.

Remember the syllabus pairs exactly: Harmattan haze and water paints are suspensions, while fog, milk, blood, aerosol spray, emulsion paints and rubber solution are colloids. True solutions such as sugar water or salt water pass filter paper and show no Tyndall beam. Checking size, settling and filtration together prevents the common swap of colloid for suspension.
bullets: Solubility is the maximum; concentration is what is present.
Downward curves mean gases; upward curves mean most salts.
Suspensions settle and block; colloids scatter and resist filtration.
Learn the syllabus examples as a fixed list.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
lessons.objective: Classify reactions in terms of oxidation and reduction in their three senses (oxygen, hydrogen/electron transfer, oxidation number), deduce oxidation numbers, balance simple redox equations, compute electrons transferred, name species and agents, and apply oxidation numbers in naming inorganic compounds.

content.heading: Oxidation and redox
paragraphs: A piece of hot copper is oxidised by oxygen, then restored by hydrogen. JAMB asks whether such a change is oxidation or reduction. This lesson gives three tests, in oxygen, electrons and oxidation numbers, for deciding correctly.

content.heading: From oxygen to electrons
paragraphs: Hot copper foil turns black in air because 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO forms CuO. Copper has gained oxygen, so it has been oxidised. Hydrogen turns CuO back to copper by removing oxygen as CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, so reduction removes oxygen with hydrogen.

Sodium is oxidised as Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ because it loses an electron, while chlorine is reduced as Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ because it gains that electron. OIL RIG says oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.
bullets: Oxidation as oxygen gain: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO, while reduction removes oxygen with H2
Oxidation as electron loss: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, while reduction gains electrons: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons
content.takeaway: Oxidation gains oxygen or loses electrons; reduction removes oxygen or gains electrons.

check.question: In the reaction 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO, copper is
options: unchanged because oxygen is a spectator
check.why: Copper gains oxygen, and also loses electrons, so it is oxidised.

content.heading: Counting oxidation numbers
paragraphs: A chemist meets potassium manganate(VII), sulphuric acid and dichromate in the same titration set. Oxidation number is a bookkeeping charge assigned by fixed rules: a free element is 0, a monatomic ion equals its charge, hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2, while the sum for a compound is 0. Applying those rules turns each colour change into a charge change that can be compared.
Manganese in KMnO4 obeys 1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7. Sulphur in H2SO4 obeys 2 + S − 8 = 0, so S = +6. Chromium in Cr2O7²⁻ obeys 2Cr − 14 = −2, so Cr = +6.
bullets: Free element is 0, and a monatomic ion takes its charge
Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2 in most compounds
Oxidation numbers sum to 0, or to the ion charge
content.takeaway: Oxidation numbers follow fixed rules, so each atom has a charge to track.

check.question: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2SO4?
check.why: 2 + S − 8 = 0 gives S = +6.

content.heading: Balancing, naming and agents
paragraphs: Purple potassium manganate(VII) turns pale green with acid and iron(II) salt. Manganese falls from +7 in MnO4⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺ and gains five electrons, while each iron rises from +2 to +3 and loses one electron. Balanced equation: MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O, with five electrons transferred.

Iron at +2 with chloride is iron(II) chloride, while iron at +3 is iron(III) chloride. Potassium manganate(VII) is an oxidising agent: purple MnO4⁻ bleaches to colourless Mn²⁺ when it is reduced. Orange acidified dichromate turns green to Cr³⁺, which also shows an oxidising agent at work.
bullets: Naming follows the ion charge: FeCl2 is iron(II) chloride and FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride
Oxidising agent is reduced while it oxidises another species; reducing agent is oxidised
Tests: purple MnO4⁻ bleaches to colourless Mn²⁺, and orange acidified dichromate turns green to Cr³⁺
content.takeaway: Rise in oxidation number is oxidation; a fall is reduction, and agents prove it.

check.question: In MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O, which species is the oxidising agent?
check.why: MnO4⁻ is reduced from +7 to +2, so it oxidises Fe²⁺.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Look first at oxidation numbers, not at oxygen. If the number rises, call it oxidation even when no oxygen appears; if it falls, call it reduction. Naming iron(II) or iron(III) is then decided by the charge that balances the chloride ions.

content.problem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2S2O3 (thiosulphuric acid)?

steps.reason: Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2, so they are known first.
Oxidation numbers sum to zero in a neutral acid.
Two sulphur atoms share the remaining charge.

content.question: What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?
hints: Assign potassium +1 and oxygen −2 first
Solve 2Cr = 12 and check the sign

content.heading: Go deeper: Why oxidation number is bookkeeping, not real charge
paragraphs: Manganese in potassium manganate(VII) carries the formal number +7, but no Mn7+ ion exists in the solution. The +7 is obtained by pretending that every bond is fully ionic and giving both shared electrons to the more electronegative partner. In a real manganese-oxygen bond electrons are shared, so manganese keeps some electron density and its physical charge is far smaller than +7.

The rule assigns electrons to the atom whose nucleus attracts them more strongly. Oxygen, being more electronegative than carbon, receives all electrons in each carbon-oxygen bond of carbon dioxide. That assignment gives oxygen −2 and carbon +4, even though the molecule is neutral and no C4+ ion is present. The numbers are correct for electron counting, not for describing isolated ions.

Because the method is a convention, special cases need memorised exceptions. Hydrogen peroxide holds oxygen at −1 rather than −2 because the two oxygen atoms share electrons equally in the oxygen-oxygen bond. Metal hydrides such as sodium hydride place hydrogen at −1 rather than +1 because hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal. Those exceptions do not break the system; they complete it.
bullets: Bookkeeping assigns bonded electrons to the more electronegative atom
Formal charge in covalent molecules need not equal a real ion charge
Peroxide oxygen is −1 and hydride hydrogen is −1, not the usual values

content.heading: Go deeper: Balancing half-equations step by step
paragraphs: Start with the two half-equations written from oxidation numbers. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, so the manganese half-equation must gain electrons: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O. Iron rises from +2 to +3, so the iron half-equation must lose electrons: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Both halves already show the correct connectivity.

Electrons gained must equal electrons lost, so the iron half-equation is multiplied by five. Five iron(II) ions give five iron(III) ions and release five electrons: 5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻. The five electrons on each side now cancel when the halves are added. Adding the halves gives MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O.

Check the finished equation for atoms and charge before writing it in an answer. Atoms: one manganese, five iron, eight hydrogen and four oxygen appear on each side. Charge: minus one plus ten plus eight equals plus seventeen on the left, and plus two plus fifteen equals plus seventeen on the right. Any mismatch shows that water, hydrogen ions or electrons have been missed.
bullets: Gain of electrons is reduction; loss of electrons is oxidation
Multiply the one-electron iron half-equation by five to match five electrons gained
Balance oxygen with water, hydrogen with H+, then cancel electrons

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in oxidation and agents
paragraphs: The most common trap confuses oxidation with the oxidising agent. Oxidation is the process in which a species rises in oxidation number, while the oxidising agent is the species that causes that rise and is itself reduced. In the iron reaction, iron(II) is oxidised and manganate(VII) is the oxidising agent because manganese falls from +7 to +2. Naming both at once prevents the reversal.

A second trap reverses the oxidation number rule. An increase in oxidation number is oxidation, and a decrease is reduction, whether or not oxygen appears. Hydrogen in copper oxide reduction rises from 0 in H2 to +1 in H2O, so hydrogen is oxidised while copper falls from +2 to 0 and is reduced. Checking the direction first settles the label.

A third trap trusts only the oxygen test and misses electron transfer entirely. Sodium forms sodium chloride with no oxygen present, yet sodium is oxidised as it loses an electron and chlorine is reduced as it gains one. JAMB sets the same pair in different formulae, so the electron and oxidation number tests must be applied beside the oxygen test. That combined habit removes the oxygen-only error.
bullets: Oxidation is the rise; the oxidising agent is reduced
Decrease in oxidation number is reduction, even without oxygen
Reducing agent is oxidised while it reduces another species

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
lessons.objective: Distinguish the properties of acids and bases, determine basicity, classify normal, acidic, basic and double salts, state methods of preparing salts, relate conductance to degree of dissociation, perform pH and pOH calculations, state the significance of pH, apply buffer solutions, choose indicators, and balance the hydrolysis of salts.

content.heading: Acids, Bases and Salts
paragraphs: A housewife in Onitsha adds vinegar to remove a stain but avoids touching a caustic soda spill on her hands. One is an acid, the other a base. What separates them is how each behaves in water.

content.heading: What acids and bases do
paragraphs: An acid is a substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions, or a proton donor. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid, for example an oxide or a hydroxide. Acids turn blue litmus red and form salts with metals and carbonates.

Bases feel soapy, turn red litmus blue and form salts with acids. The number of replaceable hydrogen atoms an acid has is its basicity, so HCl is monobasic while H₂SO₄ is dibasic. Acids and bases therefore cancel each other in neutralisation.

Indicators tell the difference without tasting anything. Litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are the standard trio, and a buffer solution is a mixture that resists pH change when acid or alkali is added. Vinegar contains ethanoic acid, while citrus fruits contain citric acid.
bullets: An acid furnishes H₃O⁺; a base neutralises an acid
Basicity counts the replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule
Litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are standard indicators
A buffer solution resists change in pH
content.takeaway: Acids donate protons, bases accept them, and indicators show which is which.

check.question: Which definition of an acid follows the proton-donor idea?
options: A substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions
A substance that turns red litmus blue
A substance that neutralises an acid
A substance that conducts electricity only when molten
check.why: Furnishing H₃O⁺ is exactly donating a proton to water.

content.heading: Salts and how they are made
paragraphs: A salt is the neutral product of reacting an acid with a base, metal or carbonate. When all replaceable hydrogen is used, the salt is normal, like NaCl. When some remains, it is acidic, like NH₄Cl, while basic salts still carry OH.

A double salt holds two salts together, and alums are the example. Salts are prepared by neutralisation, by precipitation, or by dissolving a metal or carbonate in an acid. Zn + dilute H₂SO₄ gives ZnSO₄ and hydrogen.

Whether a solution conducts depends on how far it dissociates. A strong acid like HCl dissociates fully and conducts well, while a weak acid like ethanoic acid dissociates partly and conducts weakly. Concentration is about how much is present, not how strongly it dissociates.
bullets: Normal salts use all replaceable hydrogen; acidic salts keep some
Alums are double salts crystallised together
Salts are prepared by neutralisation, precipitation or acid on metal
Conductance follows the amount of ions, not just concentration
content.takeaway: Salt type names its leftover hydrogen or hydroxide, and strength means dissociation.

check.question: NH₄Cl is an example of which salt type?
check.why: Ammonium chloride carries replaceable hydrogen, so it is an acidic salt.
